drivingQuestion: When no blood emerged during the slaughter, is the meat rendered susceptible to ritual impurity — and may it therefore be eaten with unwashed hands?
outcomeNote: A mishna stating a rule with a single named dissent; no gemara in this unit and no resolution is offered.

segments.he: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹחֵט בְּהֵמָה חַיָּה וָעוֹף וְלֹא יָצָא מֵהֶן דָּם – כְּשֵׁרִים, וְנֶאֱכָלִין בְּיָדַיִם מְסוֹאָבוֹת, לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הוּכְשְׁרוּ בַּדָּם. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: הוּכְשְׁרוּ בַּשְּׁחִיטָה.
segments.en: «MISHNA:» In the case of «one who slaughters a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal, or a bird, and blood did not emerge from them» during the slaughter, all of these are «permitted» for consumption «and» do not require the ritual washing of the hands as «they may be eaten with ritually impure [mesoavot] hands, because they were not rendered susceptible» to ritual impurity through contact «with blood,» which is one of the seven liquids that render food susceptible to impurity. «Rabbi Shimon says: They were rendered susceptible» to ritual impurity «by means of» the «slaughter» itself.

moves.cueHe: השוחט בהמה חיה ועוף ולא יצא מהן דם – כשרים
moves.summary: the slaughter is valid and the meat may be eaten with unwashed hands, not having been made susceptible by blood
moves.about: why such meat may be eaten with unwashed hands — because blood, one of the seven liquids that render food susceptible, never touched it

moves.summary: Rabbi Shimon holds the slaughter itself renders the meat susceptible to impurity
moves.about: whether an animal slaughtered without blood emerging is rendered susceptible to ritual impurity — the first tanna says it is not, since nothing was made susceptible by blood, while Rabbi Shimon says the act of slaughter itself renders it susceptible
